## A Short Defense of Getting Lost

There is a particular kind of freedom in missing the turn you meant to take.

We are taught to admire efficiency: the fastest route, the shortest line, the task completed before the day has properly begun. A map is a promise. A route is a sentence. But a detour is a question—and questions have a way of leading somewhere sentences never could.

So suppose you leave the station with enough time to spare and, for reasons that are perfectly sensible at the moment, turn left instead of right. Suddenly there is a street you have never seen. A cat sleeps in a window box. A baker is pulling loaves from an oven, and the warm smell of bread drifts into the cold air like an invitation. Someone has painted a small blue door on a wall, though the door itself may have disappeared years ago.

None of this was on your itinerary.

That is rather the point.

Much of life is experienced through narrowed attention. We look for what we expect to find, hear what confirms what we already know, walk through familiar rooms while our minds are elsewhere. Being lost—or briefly pretending to be lost—loosens that grip. The world stops being scenery and becomes an event.

At the same time, there is something worthwhile in the way an uncertain street asks us to become observers again. You notice the cracked paving stones, the upstairs window propped open with a folded newspaper, the handwriting on a café chalkboard. You hear a bicycle bell somewhere behind you. You smell rain arriving from several blocks away.

The destination, when you finally reach it, is only one version of what happened.

The other versions are waiting in side streets: the conversation that might have happened, the book discovered in an unremarkable shop, the view that would have changed if you had chosen the other path. Life is full of these invisible rooms. We cannot enter all of them. Perhaps no one can. But getting lost, even for ten minutes, reminds us that they exist.

Not every detour deserves a philosophy. Sometimes a wrong turn is simply a wrong turn, and it is wise to ask someone for directions. Still, the world is larger than our plans, and our plans are smaller than the world.

The shortest path is not always the richest one.
